persons.name: A O T Breed

occupation.note: No source in this pass's evidence records an occupation for this person. A poll list, a tax list, a muster roll and a baptismal entry each print a name and no trade, and where a later directory prints one it is a trade of 1843 — T-0633 is the rule for back-projecting that, and this pass does not have it.

persons.note: A CONTEMPORARY CHICAGO PAPER OF 1833-1835 PRINTS THIS PERSON BY NAME IN THE TOWN. Read from newspaper_1833_1835. THE GRADE IS THE OWNER'S RATIFIED LADDER OF 2026-09-03 (G1b), applied to every identity at once by tools/consolidate_resident_evidence.py and spent onto this card by tools/mint_civic_residents.py; the evidence blocks below carry the reading AS READ, its locator and the record it came from, so the page can be gone back to. WHAT IS RECONSTRUCTED: everything except the person and the sources — no dwelling, no trade, no origin, no family, no party. A BOUND FROM THE RECORD, NOT AN ARRIVAL. newspaper_1833_1835 names this person at Chicago by 4 February 1834 and nothing says when they came. The bound is at or before the scene date, so the person was at Chicago by 1 July 1835 on this record's own evidence. No figure is drawn (L1). THE SECOND PRESBYTERIAN ROLL — A NAME ON A CHURCH LIST THAT OPENS IN 1842, AND NEVER AN 1835 FACT. The 1892 printed membership roll of the Second Presbyterian Church of Chicago, read line by line into this repository, carries 1 line whose surname and given initial agree with this person's — “Breed, Mrs. Amanda | Letter. | January 12, 1877. | Dismissed.” (second_presb_0432, printed page 179), admitted 1877-01-12 by letter. Under the rule that decided it: Surname 'Breed' folds to the same string as the roll line's, and the given name of both begins A. WHAT THE MATCH MINTS OR REGRADES: “NOTHING. A line on a roll that opens in June 1842 cannot place a person in the town of July 1835, and this file makes no proposal that it does. What a match IS: the same surname and initial, in Chicago, within seven years — a lead for a later pass that is allowed to write people.” THE LINE IS A MARRIED WOMAN'S ENTRY, and the crosswalk's own Mrs rule governs what it can have met: “a line flagged a_married_womans_entry that meets a MAN in the 1835 layer has met his name, not him: it corroborates that the name was a Chicago name in the 1840s and it does not put that man on this roll.” The match is filed rather than suppressed, because a suppressed match is invisible and a flagged one can be argued with. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE: under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the roll is handed to the card as a thing a reader may weigh, and the verdict stays with T-0515, which applies the ladder against every source at once.

merge_ruling.for_merge: THREE INITIALS AGREEING IN ORDER IS AS DISTINCTIVE AS A FORENAME GETS. 'A. O. T.' is not J. or W. H.; the corpus holds no second bearer of those three initials under any surname. A. O. T. Breed is a documented man of the county: the Democrat prints a writ 'dated the 20th day of [March, A.] D. 1834, at the suit of A. O. T. Bre[ed, of the said] county of Cook, and State of Illinois' against an estate in the Territory of Michigan for $1,014; it prints 'Cook Circuit Court, May Term, 1834. Bristol, Howard & Wadham[s] vs. A. O. T. Breed'; the letter list of 1 January 1834 carries him; the Second Presbyterian roll carries the surname. A man suing and sued in the county's own court in 1834 is a man who could be expected on the town's poll of 1835, and the only entry on that poll that could be him is 'Bread, A.O.T.'
merge_ruling.against_merge: NO TITLE REACHED SETS BOTH SPELLINGS, AND ONE OF THEM IS SET EXACTLY ONCE IN THE WHOLE CORPUS. Searched word-boundary over every deposited text and every extracted claim: 'Bread' occurs as a SURNAME in exactly one place — the 1835 poll list, 'Bread, A.O.T.' (voter_lists_1833_1835.txt lines 289 and 294, the transcription printing the page twice) — and every other hit in the corpus is the common noun, including Moses & Kirkland's index entry 'Bread, limitation of, price'. 'Breed' is set by the Democrat, by the Second Presbyterian roll ('Breed, Mrs. Amanda'), by genealogytrails' cemetery history and by Moses & Kirkland — and never beside 'Bread'. The two bodies of evidence do not touch: the town's own roll knows only Bread, and the press, the church and the books know only Breed. Folding on what is left — one letter — is what T-1001 measured and refused. D7, and the cards stay two. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT IS NOT A PAGE BUT A COUNT, in C12's shape moved from the forename to the surname — the closed roll leaves the documented man exactly one entry he can be, and the exhaustion is worked over the whole roll and printed rather than asserted. C12 as written reaches a FORENAME only, so firing it on a surname is itself a rule to write. T-1135 owns that question for Pruyne/Pryne and the rule it writes is the one this pair waits on.

roles.note: PRINTED AGAINST THIS NAME IN THE 1833-1835 PRESS and carried here from the newspaper gazetteer (T-1254, by tools/derive_resident_roles.py). The gazetteer holds its trades on the PERSON record and not on a single issue, so the bound is the run of this person's own dated mentions, 1834-02-04 to 1834-04-16, and the grade is `inferred`: the paper printed the trade, and the resident programme's identity rule tied the printing to this card. The scene date falls outside that run, so this role does not stand in the 1835 view.

age_band.note: AN AGE BAND, NEVER A YEAR. No source this project holds bears on when this person was born, so the band is drawn from the only committed sex by age distribution the project has - the 1840 Chicago schedule, five years after the scene and a town twice the size - seeded by this person's own id ('breed_a_o_t:age_bands_1840'). AND THE CONDITIONING IS THE MODEL'S, NOT A SOURCE'S: that a roll naming a person in their own right names somebody 15 or over. The 1840 schedule counts a child as a tally inside a household and never as a correspondent; 15 rather than 20 because an apprentice or a journeyman stands on a trade roll. No source states this rule. No exact year is written, because a year drawn from a decadal band would read as a record of a birth.
